parts.text:
"You are inspecting a Python project inside a container at /app.

READ ONLY. Do not create, modify or delete any file under /app.
Any write there invalidates this run.

A developer is about to work on the task described below.

\"
<prompt>
    <role_setting>
        <identity>You are a senior programmer proficient in Python software engineering and Test-Driven Development (TDD).</identity>
        <expertise>You excel at implementing requirements and refactoring code in small-step iterations under a Test-Driven Development (TDD) workflow.</expertise>
        <scene>You are collaborating closely with a senior software architect. The architect produces incremental requirement documents based on the functional gaps of the current code; you are responsible for understanding the content of this document and implementing the requirements to change the status of target tests from non-passed to passed.</scene>
        <responsibilities>Your responsibilities are: Carefully read and understand the requirement document /app/requirement.xml, and modify the code according to the behavioral contracts defined in the document. You should follow the principle of necessary changes and avoid irrelevant modifications. You are prohibited from executing test actively.</responsibilities>
    </role_setting>

    <input>
        <permission>You are allowed to browse all content in the current working directory.</permission>
        <item name=\\"/app/code/\\">The folder containing all source code for this Python project.</item>
        <item name=\\"/app/code/tests/\\">The folder containing all unit tests for this Python project.</item>
        <item name=\\"/app/requirement.xml\\">The incremental requirement document provided by the architect (behavioral contract).</item>
    </input>

    <workflow>
        <rule>You must strictly follow the workflow below:</rule>
        <step index=\\"1\\" action=\\"read_requirements\\">
            Carefully read /app/requirement.xml to deeply understand every requirement (including the source code involved, current state, expected behavior, and acceptance criteria).
        </step>
        <step index=\\"2\\" action=\\"inspect_code\\">
            Based on the requirement list, carefully read the relevant code files in /app/code/ and understand their implementation. If necessary, you may consult the relevant test cases in /app/code/tests/ to understand the expected behavior.
        </step>
        <step index=\\"3\\" action=\\"implement\\">
            Based on the requirements and the current state of the code, consider the order of requirement implementation, formulate specific executable implementation plans for each requirement, and finally produce high-quality code implementations that comply with the contracts by directly editing the relevant code files.
        </step>
    </workflow>

    <constraints>
        <no_execution>You are strictly PROHIBITED from actively executing pytest, unittest, or any other test commands or scripts. Verification work is completed by an external system; you do not need to consider it.</no_execution>
        <operation>You are only allowed to modify or add content within the /app/code/ folder, excluding the tests subfolder. It is strictly PROHIBITED to make any changes to the /app/requirement.xml file or the /app/code/tests/ folder.</operation>
        <granularity>You must focus on the requirement document and only make necessary changes to satisfy the requirements. You should not expand the scope on your own or over-develop.</granularity>
    </constraints>

    <output>
        <product>Your modified codebase (changes under /app/code/). Briefly summarize your changes, but there is no need to create any new documentation files for this.</product>
    </output>
</prompt>

\"

Read enough of /app/code to answer concretely, then name 3 to 5
plausible FUTURE tasks that could reasonably follow this one in THIS codebase.
Refer to real files, functions or modules you actually read. Do not solve the
task, and do not write any file."

5: # %% [markdown]
6: """
7: # Expression
8: 
9: [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/expression.svg)](https://pypi.python.org/pypi/Expression)
10: ![Python package](https://github.com/cognitedata/expression/workflows/Python%20package/badge.svg)
11: [![Publish Package](https://github.com/dbrattli/Expression/actions/workflows/python-publish.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/dbrattli/Expression/actions/workflows/python-publish.yml)
12: [![Documentation Status](https://readthedocs.org/projects/expression/badge/?version=latest)](https://expression.readthedocs.io/en/latest/?badge=latest)
13: [![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/cognitedata/expression/branch/main/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/cognitedata/expression)
14: 
15: > Pragmatic functional programming
16: """
17: 
18: # %% [markdown]
19: """
20: Expression aims to be a solid, type-safe, pragmatic, and high performance library for
21: frictionless and practical functional programming in Python 3.10+.
22: 
23: By pragmatic, we mean that the goal of the library is to use simple abstractions to
24: enable you to do practical and productive functional programming in Python (instead of
25: being a [Monad tutorial](https://github.com/dbrattli/OSlash)).
26: 
27: Python is a multi-paradigm programming language that also supports functional
28: programming constructs such as functions, higher-order functions, lambdas, and in many
29: ways favors composition over inheritance.
30: 
31: > Better Python with F#
32: 
33: Expression tries to make a better Python by providing several functional features
34: inspired by [F#](https://fsharp.org). This serves several purposes:
35: 
36: - Enable functional programming in a Pythonic way, i.e., make sure we are not
37:   over-abstracting things. Expression will not require purely functional programming as
38:   would a language like Haskell.
39: - Everything you learn with Expression can also be used with F#. Learn F# by starting in
40:   a programming language they already know. Perhaps get inspired to also [try out
41:   F#](https://aka.ms/fsharphome) by itself.
42: - Make it easier for F# developers to use Python when needed, and re-use many of the
43:   concepts and abstractions they already know and love.
44: 
45: Expression will enable you to work with Python using many of the same programming
46: concepts and abstractions. This enables concepts such as [Railway oriented
47: programming](https://fsharpforfunandprofit.com/rop/) (ROP) for better and predictable
48: error handling. Pipelining for workflows, computational expressions, etc.
49: 
50: > _Expressions evaluate to a value. Statements do something._
51: 
52: F# is a functional programming language for .NET that is succinct (concise, readable,
53: and type-safe) and kind of [Pythonic](https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html). F# is in
54: many ways very similar to Python, but F# can also do a lot of things better than Python:
55: 
56: - Strongly typed, if it compiles it usually works making refactoring much safer. You can
57:   trust the type-system. With [mypy](http://mypy-lang.org/) or
58:   [Pylance](https://github.com/microsoft/pylance-release) you often wonder who is right
59:   and who is wrong.
60: - Type inference, the compiler deduces types during compilation
61: - Expression based language
62: """
63: 
64: # %% [markdown]
65: """
66: ## Getting Started
67: 
68: You can install the latest `expression` from PyPI by running `pip` (or
69: `pip3`). Note that `expression` only works for Python 3.10+.
70: 
71: ```console
72: > pip install expression
73: ```
74: 
75: To add Pydantic v2 support, install the `pydantic` extra:
76: 
77: ```console
78: > pip install expression[pydantic]
79: ```
80: """
81: 
82: # %% [markdown]
83: """
84: ## Goals
85: 
86: - Industrial strength library for functional programming in Python.
87: - The resulting code should look and feel like Python
88:   ([PEP-8](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0008/)). We want to make a
89:   better Python, not some obscure DSL or academic Monad tutorial.
90: - Provide pipelining and pipe friendly methods. Compose all the things!
91: - Dot-chaining on objects as an alternative syntax to pipes.
92: - Lower the cognitive load on the programmer by:
93:   - Avoid currying, not supported in Python by default and not a well known
94:     concept by Python programmers.
95:   - Avoid operator (`|`, `>>`, etc) overloading, this usually confuses more
96:     than it helps.
97:   - Avoid recursion. Recursion is not normally used in Python and any use of it
98:     should be hidden within the SDK.
99: - Provide [type-hints](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html) for all
100:   functions and methods.
101: - Support PEP 634 and structural pattern matching.
102: - Code must pass strict static type checking by
103:   [Pylance](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/python/announcing-pylance-fast-feature-rich-language-support-for-python-in-visual-studio-code/).
104:   Pylance is awesome, use it!
105: - [Pydantic](https://pydantic-docs.helpmanual.io/) friendly data types. Use Expression
106:   types as part of your Pydantic data model and (de)serialize to/from JSON.
107: """
108: 
109: # %% [markdown]
110: """
111: ## Supported features
112: 
113: Expression will never provide you with all the features of F# and .NET. We are
114: providing a few of the features we think are useful, and will add more
115: on-demand as we go along.
116: 
117: - **Pipelining** - for creating workflows.
118: - **Composition** - for composing and creating new operators.
119: - **Fluent or Functional** syntax, i.e., dot chain or pipeline operators.
120: - **Pattern Matching** - an alternative flow control to `if-elif-else`.
121: - **Error Handling** - Several error handling types.
122:   - **Option** - for optional stuff and better `None` handling.
123:   - **Result** - for better error handling and enables railway-oriented
124:     programming in Python.
125:   - **Try** - a simpler result type that pins the error to an Exception.
126: - **Collections** - immutable collections.
127:   - **TypedArray** - a generic array type that abstracts the details of
128:     `bytearray`, `array.array` and `list` modules.
129:   - **Sequence** - a better
130:     [itertools](https://docs.python.org/3/library/itertools.html) and
131:     fully compatible with Python iterables.
132:   - **Block** - a frozen and immutable list type.
133:   - **Map** - a frozen and immutable dictionary type.
134:   - **AsyncSeq** - Asynchronous iterables.
135:   - **AsyncObservable** - Asynchronous observables. Provided separately
136:     by [aioreactive](https://github.com/dbrattli/aioreactive).
137: - **Data Modeling** - sum and product types
138:   - **@tagged_union** - A tagged (discriminated) union type decorator.
139: - **Parser Combinators** - A recursive decent string parser combinator
140:   library.
141: - **Effects**: - lightweight computational expressions for Python. This
142:   is amazing stuff.
143:   - **option** - an optional world for working with optional values.
144:   - **result** - an error handling world for working with result values.
145: - **Mailbox Processor**: for lock free programming using the [Actor
146:   model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actor_model).
147: - **Cancellation Token**: for cancellation of asynchronous (and
148:   synchronous) workflows.
149: - **Disposable**: For resource management.
150: """
151: 
152: # %% [markdown]
153: """
154: ### Pipelining
155: 
156: Expression provides a `pipe` function similar to `|>` in F#. We don't want to overload
157: any Python operators, e.g., `|` so `pipe` is a plain old function taking N-arguments,
158: and will let you pipe a value through any number of functions.
159: """
160: 
161: # %%
162: from collections.abc import Callable
163: 
164: from expression import pipe
165: 
166: 
167: v = 1
168: fn1: Callable[[int], int] = lambda x: x + 1
169: gn1: Callable[[int], int] = lambda x: x * 2
170: 
171: assert pipe(v, fn1, gn1) == gn1(fn1(v))
172: 
173: # %% [markdown]
174: """
175: Expression objects (e.g., `Some`, `Seq`, `Result`) also have a `pipe` method, so you can
176: dot chain pipelines directly on the object:
177: """
178: 
179: # %%
180: from expression import Option, Some
181: 
182: 
183: v = Some(1)
184: fn2: Callable[[Option[int]], Option[int]] = lambda x: x.map(lambda y: y + 1)
185: gn2: Callable[[Option[int]], Option[int]] = lambda x: x.map(lambda y: y * 2)
186: 
187: assert v.pipe(fn2, gn2) == gn2(fn2(v))
188: 
189: # %% [markdown]
190: """
191: So for example with sequences you may create sequence transforming
192: pipelines:
193: """
194: 
195: # %%
196: from collections.abc import Callable
197: 
198: from expression.collections import Seq, seq
199: 
200: 
201: # Since static type checkes aren't good good at inferring lambda types
202: mapper: Callable[[int], int] = lambda x: x * 10
203: predicate: Callable[[int], bool] = lambda x: x > 100
204: folder: Callable[[int, int], int] = lambda s, x: s + x
205: 
206: xs = Seq.of(9, 10, 11)
207: ys = xs.pipe(
208:     seq.map(mapper),
209:     seq.filter(predicate),
210:     seq.fold(folder, 0),
211: )
212: 
213: assert ys == 110
214: 
215: # %% [markdown]
216: """
217: ### Composition
218: 
219: Functions may even be composed directly into custom operators:
220: """
221: 
222: # %%
223: from expression import compose
224: from expression.collections import Seq, seq
225: 
226: 
227: mapper: Callable[[int], int] = lambda x: x * 10
228: predicate: Callable[[int], bool] = lambda x: x > 100
229: folder: Callable[[int, int], int] = lambda s, x: s + x
230: 
231: xs = Seq.of(9, 10, 11)
232: custom = compose(
233:     seq.map(mapper),
234:     seq.filter(predicate),
235:     seq.fold(folder, 0),
236: )
237: ys = custom(xs)
238: 
239: assert ys == 110
240: 
241: # %% [markdown]
242: """
243: ### Fluent and Functional
244: 
245: Expression can be used both with a fluent or functional syntax (or both.)
246: 
247: #### Fluent syntax
248: 
249: The fluent syntax uses methods and is very compact. But it might get you into
250: trouble for large pipelines since it's not a natural way of adding line breaks.
251: """
252: 
253: # %%
254: from expression.collections import Seq
255: 
256: 
257: xs = Seq.of(1, 2, 3)
258: ys = xs.map(lambda x: x * 100).filter(lambda x: x > 100).fold(lambda s, x: s + x, 0)
259: 
260: # %% [markdown]
261: """
262: Note that fluent syntax is probably the better choice if you use mypy
263: for type checking since mypy may have problems inferring types through
264: larger pipelines.
265: 
266: #### Functional syntax
267: 
268: The functional syntax is a bit more verbose but you can easily add new
269: operations on new lines. The functional syntax is great to use together
270: with pylance/pyright.
271: """
272: 
273: # %%
274: from expression import pipe
275: from expression.collections import Seq, seq
276: 
277: 
278: mapper: Callable[[int], int] = lambda x: x * 100
279: 
280: xs = Seq.of(1, 2, 3)
281: ys = pipe(
282:     xs,
283:     seq.map(mapper),
284:     seq.filter(lambda x: x > 100),
285:     seq.fold(lambda s, x: s + x, 0),
286: )
287: 
288: # %% [markdown]
289: """
290: Both fluent and functional syntax may be mixed and even pipe can be used
291: fluently.
292: 
293: ```python
294: from expression.collections import seq, Seq
295: xs = Seq.of(1, 2, 3).pipe(seq.map(...))
296: ```
297: """
298: 
299: # %% [markdown]
300: """
301: ### Option
302: 
303: The `Option` type is used when a function or method cannot produce a meaningful
304: output for a given input.
305: 
306: An option value may have a value of a given type, i.e., `Some(value)`, or it might
307: not have any meaningful value, i.e., `Nothing`.
308: """
309: 
310: # %%
311: from expression import Nothing, Option, Some
312: 
313: 
314: def keep_positive(a: int) -> Option[int]:
315:     if a > 0:
316:         return Some(a)
317: 
318:     return Nothing
319: 
320: 
321: # %%
322: from typing import Literal
323: 
324: from expression import Ok, Option
325: 
326: 
327: def exists(x: Option[int]) -> bool:
328:     match x:
329:         case Option(tag="some"):
330:             return True
331:         case _:
332:             return False
333: 
334: 
335: # %% [markdown]
336: """
337: ### Option as an effect
338: 
339: Effects in Expression is implemented as specially decorated coroutines
340: ([enhanced generators](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0342/)) using
341: `yield`, `yield from` and `return` to consume or generate optional values:
342: """
343: 
344: # %%
345: from collections.abc import Generator
346: 
347: from expression import Some, effect
348: 
349: 
350: @effect.option[int]()
351: def fn3() -> Generator[int, int, int]:
352:     x = yield 42
353:     y = yield from Some(43)
354: 
355:     return x + y
356: 
357: 
358: xs = fn3()
359: 
360: # %% [markdown]
361: """
362: This enables ["railway oriented
363: programming"](https://fsharpforfunandprofit.com/rop/), e.g., if one part of the
364: function yields from `Nothing` then the function is side-tracked
365: (short-circuit) and the following statements will never be executed. The end
366: result of the expression will be `Nothing`. Thus results from such an option
367: decorated function can either be `Ok(value)` or `Error(error_value)`.
368: """
369: 
370: # %%
371: from collections.abc import Generator
372: 
373: from expression import Nothing, Some, effect
374: 
375: 
376: @effect.option[int]()
377: def fn4() -> Generator[int, int, int]:
378:     x = yield from Nothing  # or a function returning Nothing
379: 
380:     # -- The rest of the function will never be executed --
381:     y = yield from Some(43)
382: 
383:     return x + y
384: 
385: 
386: xs = fn4()
387: assert xs is Nothing
388: 
389: # %% [markdown]
390: """
391: ### Option as an applicative
392: 
393: In functional programming, we sometimes want to combine two Option values into a new
394: Option. However, this combination should only happen if both Options are Some. If either
395: Option is None, the resulting value should also be None.
396: 
397: The map2 function allows us to achieve this behavior. It takes two Option values and a
398: function as arguments. The function is applied only if both Options are Some, and the
399: result becomes the new Some value. Otherwise, map2 returns None.
400: 
401: This approach ensures that our combined value reflects the presence or absence of data
402: in the original Options.
403: """
404: 
405: # %%
406: from operator import add
407: 
408: from expression import Nothing, Option, Some
409: 
410: 
411: def keep_positive(a: int) -> Option[int]:
412:     if a > 0:
413:         return Some(a)
414:     else:
415:         return Nothing
416: 
417: 
418: def add_options(a: Option[int], b: Option[int]):
419:     return a.map2(add, b)
420: 
421: 
422: assert add_options(keep_positive(4), keep_positive(-2)) is Nothing
423: 
424: assert add_options(keep_positive(3), keep_positive(2)) == Some(5)
425: 
426: # %% [markdown]
427: """
428: For more information about options:
429: 
430: - [Tutorial](https://expression.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorial/optional_values.html)
431: - [API reference](https://expression.readthedocs.io/en/latest/reference/option.html)
432: """
433: 
434: # %% [markdown]
435: """
436: ### Result
437: 
438: The `Result[T, TError]` type lets you write error-tolerant code that can be composed. A
439: Result works similar to `Option`, but lets you define the value used for errors, e.g.,
440: an exception type or similar. This is great when you want to know why some operation
441: failed (not just `Nothing`). This type serves the same purpose of an `Either` type where
442: `Left` is used for the error condition and `Right` for a success value.
443: """
444: 
445: # %%
446: from expression import Ok, Result, effect
447: 
448: 
449: @effect.result[int, Exception]()
450: def fn5() -> Generator[int, int, int]:
451:     x = yield from Ok(42)
452:     y = yield from Ok(10)
453:     return x + y
454: 
455: 
456: xs = fn5()
457: assert isinstance(xs, Result)
458: 
459: # %% [markdown]
460: """
461: A simplified type called `Try` is also available. It's a result type that is
462: pinned to `Exception` i.e., `Result[TSource, Exception]`.
463: """
464: 
465: # %% [markdown]
466: """
467: ### Sequence

"""
# Expression

# %% [markdown]
"""
Expression aims to be a solid, type-safe, pragmatic, and high performance library for
frictionless and practical functional programming in Python 3.10+.

By pragmatic, we mean that the goal of the library is to use simple abstractions to
enable you to do practical and productive functional programming in Python (instead of
being a [Monad tutorial](https://github.com/dbrattli/OSlash)).

Python is a multi-paradigm programming language that also supports functional
programming constructs such as functions, higher-order functions, lambdas, and in many
ways favors composition over inheritance.

> Better Python with F#

Expression tries to make a better Python by providing several functional features
inspired by [F#](https://fsharp.org). This serves several purposes:

- Enable functional programming in a Pythonic way, i.e., make sure we are not
  over-abstracting things. Expression will not require purely functional programming as
  would a language like Haskell.
- Everything you learn with Expression can also be used with F#. Learn F# by starting in
  a programming language they already know. Perhaps get inspired to also [try out
  F#](https://aka.ms/fsharphome) by itself.
- Make it easier for F# developers to use Python when needed, and re-use many of the
  concepts and abstractions they already know and love.

Expression will enable you to work with Python using many of the same programming
concepts and abstractions. This enables concepts such as [Railway oriented
programming](https://fsharpforfunandprofit.com/rop/) (ROP) for better and predictable
error handling. Pipelining for workflows, computational expressions, etc.

> _Expressions evaluate to a value. Statements do something._

F# is a functional programming language for .NET that is succinct (concise, readable,
and type-safe) and kind of [Pythonic](https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html). F# is in
many ways very similar to Python, but F# can also do a lot of things better than Python:

- Strongly typed, if it compiles it usually works making refactoring much safer. You can
  trust the type-system. With [mypy](http://mypy-lang.org/) or
  [Pylance](https://github.com/microsoft/pylance-release) you often wonder who is right
  and who is wrong.
- Type inference, the compiler deduces types during compilation
- Expression based language
"""

# %% [markdown]
"""
## Getting Started

You can install the latest `expression` from PyPI by running `pip` (or
`pip3`). Note that `expression` only works for Python 3.10+.

```console
> pip install expression
```

To add Pydantic v2 support, install the `pydantic` extra:

```console
> pip install expression[pydantic]
```
"""

# %% [markdown]
"""
## Goals

- Industrial strength library for functional programming in Python.
- The resulting code should look and feel like Python
  ([PEP-8](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0008/)). We want to make a
  better Python, not some obscure DSL or academic Monad tutorial.
- Provide pipelining and pipe friendly methods. Compose all the things!
- Dot-chaining on objects as an alternative syntax to pipes.
- Lower the cognitive load on the programmer by:
  - Avoid currying, not supported in Python by default and not a well known
    concept by Python programmers.
  - Avoid operator (`|`, `>>`, etc) overloading, this usually confuses more
    than it helps.
  - Avoid recursion. Recursion is not normally used in Python and any use of it
    should be hidden within the SDK.
- Provide [type-hints](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html) for all
  functions and methods.
- Support PEP 634 and structural pattern matching.
- Code must pass strict static type checking by
  [Pylance](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/python/announcing-pylance-fast-feature-rich-language-support-for-python-in-visual-studio-code/).
  Pylance is awesome, use it!
- [Pydantic](https://pydantic-docs.helpmanual.io/) friendly data types. Use Expression
  types as part of your Pydantic data model and (de)serialize to/from JSON.
"""

# %% [markdown]
"""
## Supported features

Expression will never provide you with all the features of F# and .NET. We are
providing a few of the features we think are useful, and will add more
on-demand as we go along.

- **Pipelining** - for creating workflows.
- **Composition** - for composing and creating new operators.
- **Fluent or Functional** syntax, i.e., dot chain or pipeline operators.
- **Pattern Matching** - an alternative flow control to `if-elif-else`.
- **Error Handling** - Several error handling types.
  - **Option** - for optional stuff and better `None` handling.
  - **Result** - for better error handling and enables railway-oriented
    programming in Python.
  - **Try** - a simpler result type that pins the error to an Exception.
- **Collections** - immutable collections.
  - **TypedArray** - a generic array type that abstracts the details of
    `bytearray`, `array.array` and `list` modules.
  - **Sequence** - a better
    [itertools](https://docs.python.org/3/library/itertools.html) and
    fully compatible with Python iterables.
  - **Block** - a frozen and immutable list type.
  - **Map** - a frozen and immutable dictionary type.
  - **AsyncSeq** - Asynchronous iterables.
  - **AsyncObservable** - Asynchronous observables. Provided separately
    by [aioreactive](https://github.com/dbrattli/aioreactive).
- **Data Modeling** - sum and product types
  - **@tagged_union** - A tagged (discriminated) union type decorator.
- **Parser Combinators** - A recursive decent string parser combinator
  library.
- **Effects**: - lightweight computational expressions for Python. This
  is amazing stuff.
  - **option** - an optional world for working with optional values.
  - **result** - an error handling world for working with result values.
- **Mailbox Processor**: for lock free programming using the [Actor
  model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actor_model).
- **Cancellation Token**: for cancellation of asynchronous (and
  synchronous) workflows.
- **Disposable**: For resource management.
"""

# %% [markdown]
"""
### Pipelining

Expression provides a `pipe` function similar to `|>` in F#. We don't want to overload
any Python operators, e.g., `|` so `pipe` is a plain old function taking N-arguments,
and will let you pipe a value through any number of functions.
"""

# %%
from collections.abc import Callable

from expression import pipe


v = 1
fn1: Callable[[int], int] = lambda x: x + 1
gn1: Callable[[int], int] = lambda x: x * 2

assert pipe(v, fn1, gn1) == gn1(fn1(v))

dot chain pipelines directly on the object:

# %%

v = Some(1)
fn2: Callable[[Option[int]], Option[int]] = lambda x: x.map(lambda y: y + 1)

assert v.pipe(fn2, gn2) == gn2(fn2(v))

mapper: Callable[[int], int] = lambda x: x * 10

ys = xs.pipe(

    seq.filter(predicate),
    seq.fold(folder, 0),

### Composition

Functions may even be composed directly into custom operators:
"""

from expression.collections import Seq, seq

    seq.fold(folder, 0),

"""
### Fluent and Functional

Expression can be used both with a fluent or functional syntax (or both.)

The fluent syntax uses methods and is very compact. But it might get you into
trouble for large pipelines since it's not a natural way of adding line breaks.

# %%

xs = Seq.of(1, 2, 3)
ys = xs.map(lambda x: x * 100).filter(lambda x: x > 100).fold(lambda s, x: s + x, 0)

for type checking since mypy may have problems inferring types through

mapper: Callable[[int], int] = lambda x: x * 100

    xs,
    seq.map(mapper),

Both fluent and functional syntax may be mixed and even pipe can be used

not have any meaningful value, i.e., `Nothing`.

# %%

def keep_positive(a: int) -> Option[int]:
    if a > 0:

    return Nothing

"""
### Option as an effect

Effects in Expression is implemented as specially decorated coroutines

from expression import Some, effect


@effect.option[int]()
def fn3() -> Generator[int, int, int]:
    x = yield 42
    y = yield from Some(43)

from operator import add

from expression import Nothing, Option, Some


def keep_positive(a: int) -> Option[int]:

    else:

assert add_options(keep_positive(4), keep_positive(-2)) is Nothing

### Result

The `Result[T, TError]` type lets you write error-tolerant code that can be composed. A

# %%

"""Tests for async_result builder implementation."""

import asyncio
from collections.abc import AsyncGenerator
from typing import List

import pytest
from pytest import raises

from expression import effect, Ok, Error, Result
from tests.utils import CustomException


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_async_result_builder_evaluation_order():
    """Test that async_result builder evaluates computations in the correct order."""
    evaluated: List[int] = []

    @effect.async_result[int, str]()
    async def fn() -> AsyncGenerator[int, int]:
        evaluated.append(1)  # First computation
        x: int = yield 42

        evaluated.append(2)  # Second computation
        y: int = yield 43

        evaluated.append(3)  # Final computation
        yield x + y  # Instead of return, use yield for the final value

    computation = await fn()
    assert evaluated == [1, 2, 3]  # All computations ran in order
    assert computation == Ok(85)


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_async_result_builder_short_circuit():
    """Test that async_result builder properly short circuits with Error."""
    evaluated: List[int] = []

    @effect.async_result[int, str]()
    async def fn() -> AsyncGenerator[int, int]:
        evaluated.append(1)  # First computation
        x: int = yield 42

        evaluated.append(2)  # Should not reach here
        # Use await with Error to leverage the awaitable functionality
        y: int = yield await Error("error")  # Short circuits here

        evaluated.append(3)  # Should not reach here
        yield x + y  # This won't be reached

    computation = await fn()
    assert evaluated == [1, 2]  # Should run until yield Error
    assert computation == Error("error")


@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_async_result_builder_combine():
    """Test that async_result builder properly combines computations."""
    evaluated: List[int] = []

    @effect.async_result[int, str]()
    async def fn() -> AsyncGenerator[int, int]:
        evaluated.append(1)
        yield 42  # First computation

        evaluated.append(2)
        yield 43  # Second computation combined with first

        evaluated.append(3)
        yield 44  # Final result

    computation = await fn()
    assert evaluated == [1, 2, 3]  # All computations ran
    assert computation == Ok(44)  # Returns final value

async def test_async_result_builder_return_from():
    """Test that async_result builder properly handles return! (return_from)."""

    @effect.async_result[int, str]()
    async def fn() -> AsyncGenerator[int, int]:
        x: int = yield await Ok(42)
        yield x

    computation = await fn()
    match computation:
        case Result(tag="ok", ok=value):
            assert value == 42
        case _:
            assert False

    @effect.async_result[int, str]()
    async def fn() -> AsyncGenerator[int, int]:
        # Use await with Ok to leverage the awaitable functionality
        x: int = yield await Ok(42)
        yield x + 1

    computation = await fn()

async def test_async_result_builder_yield_error():
    """Test that async_result builder properly handles yielding Error."""

    @effect.async_result[int, str]()

@pytest.mark.asyncio
async def test_async_result_builder_nested():

        y: int = yield x + 1
        yield y + 1

        x: int = yield 42

        y: int = yield await inner_result  # Then yield the result
